title: Four doors, one number
told: the history and tradition of the Harmandir Sahib

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever walked into a place of worship and wondered if you were really welcome?
options: then this one is for you. listen.
then listen. this door was built for you too.
good. then you’ll know what this place feels like.

steps.line: Over four hundred years ago, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, began building a house of God in the middle of a sacred pool in Amritsar.

steps.q: Who do you think the Guru asked to lay the very first stone?
o: A Muslim holy man from Lahore
steps.why: A Sufi saint, a Muslim holy man and the Guru’s friend.

steps.line: Many Sikhs tell that he asked his friend, the Muslim saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to lay the first stone.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: And he gave it four doors, one on every side. You could walk in from any direction.

steps.q: Why give a house of God four doors, one on each side?
o: To say all are welcome, from anywhere
One for each of the first four Gurus
steps.why: Every side is a front door. Sikhs often say it means the place is open to all, whatever their faith or caste.

steps.line: Then Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus into one great book, with songs by Hindu and Muslim saints in it too.
The book opens with Guru Nanak’s symbol, Ik Onkar. Ik is written as the numeral one. Onkar is an ancient name for God.

steps.q: How is most of the great book, the Guru Granth Sahib, arranged?
o: By raga: the tune it’s sung to
By which Guru wrote each hymn
By the year each was written
steps.why: Most hymns are grouped into 31 ragas, musical modes, because the scripture is meant to be sung. Within each raga, the Gurus come first, then the other saints.

steps.line: Today, at the Golden Temple, the doors still face every way, and the great book is still carried in each morning.
steps.label: today

steps.q: You walk into a gurdwara for the first time. What will they ask of you?
o: Say whether you are a Sikh
Cover your head, take off your shoes
Pay a small offering at the door
steps.why: Anyone of any faith is welcome. Cover your head, slip off your shoes, wash your hands, and you’ll likely be offered a free meal at the langar.

say: here’s what i love. before one rule or one story, the sikh scripture says a single thing: there is one.
and if there’s one, nobody stands outside it. that’s why the doors face every way.

steps.q: From the story, why does “there is one” fit a temple with four doors and a book with Hindu and Muslim saints in it?
o: If there’s one source, nobody is an outsider
Every faith was meant to merge into one new faith
So each faith would have its own separate door
steps.why: One source, so no outsiders. Every door is for everyone, and the saints in the book kept their own names and faiths.

today.say: today, when someone gets on your nerves, think one quiet word: one. sikhs believe the same light is in them as in you.
options: good. the doors face every way.
even them. if there’s one, nobody’s outside.

card.from: the story of the Harmandir Sahib
card.keepWhy: There is one, so every side is a front door.
sources: Sikh tradition that the Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore laid the foundation stone of the Harmandir Sahib for Guru Arjan (traditionally dated 1588 or 1589)
The Harmandir Sahib built with entrances on all four sides
Guru Arjan’s compilation of the Adi Granth, installed at the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, including hymns of bhagats such as Kabir and Sheikh Farid
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Ik Onkar at the head of the Mool Mantar)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13 (“sabh meh jot jot hai soi”: in all is the light, and that light is the One)
Daily procession bringing the Guru Granth Sahib into the Harmandir Sahib each morning
check: Mian Mir laying the foundation stone is a widely told tradition but early sources are thin and it is debated; labeled “a traditional story”.
The four doors as open to all directions, faiths and castes is the common Sikh explanation; confirm framing.
